target_paper_title: An Evidence-Based Post-Hoc Adjustment Framework for Anomaly Detection Under Data Contamination

gold_annotations.topic: This paper studies unsupervised anomaly detection under contaminated training data, where the training set may already contain undetected anomalies and the deployed anomaly detector is treated as a pretrained or proprietary model that cannot be retrained easily. The setting emphasizes preparation-agnostic test-time adaptation: the goal is to improve anomaly detection at test time without access to the original training pipeline, training data, or reliable knowledge of the contamination ratio, across visual, tabular, and industrial anomaly detection scenarios.
gold_annotations.golden_gap: The paper argues that standard unsupervised anomaly detection methods usually assume clean training data, but real-world datasets are often contaminated, which biases the learned detector and degrades its ability to separate normal and anomalous instances. Existing contamination-aware methods either modify training, filter training data, or rely on prior knowledge such as the contamination ratio, and they are often computationally expensive or impractical when the detector is proprietary and internal training artifacts are unavailable. This leaves a gap for a practical post-hoc method that can improve contaminated anomaly detectors at test time without retraining and without labeled validation data.
gold_annotations.golden_method: The proposed method is EPHAD, an evidence-based post-hoc adjustment framework for anomaly detection. EPHAD keeps the original anomaly detector fixed and combines its outputs with an external evidence function computed at test time, where the evidence assigns higher values to samples judged more likely to be normal and can come from sources such as CLIP, Local Outlier Factor, Isolation Forest, or domain knowledge. The core idea is an exponential tilting update that shifts the contaminated model distribution toward evidence-favored regions while remaining close to the original model through a temperature parameter beta that controls the trade-off. The method is extended from density-based anomaly detection to the score-based setting used by modern anomaly detectors, yielding a revised inlier score obtained by combining the original inlier score with the evidence term. The paper also proposes EPHAD-Ada, an unsupervised variant that estimates beta from test-time predictive entropy so the framework can adapt its reliance on the original detector versus the evidence function without labeled validation data.
gold_annotations.gold_experiment: The paper evaluates EPHAD on multiple anomaly detection regimes: eight visual anomaly detection datasets covering both sensory and semantic anomaly detection, twenty-six tabular benchmark datasets from ADBench, and an industrial anomaly detection use case in the appendix. The experiments simulate controlled contamination in training data and compare strong unsupervised anomaly detection baselines, including PatchCore, PaDiM, CFLOW, FastFlow, DRAEM, Reverse Distillation, ULSAD, IForest, LOF, DeepSVDD, ECOD, and COPOD, with and without EPHAD. Evidence functions are also varied, including CLIP for image settings and LOF or Isolation Forest for tabular settings. Performance is mainly measured by AUROC, and the study includes a toy illustrative example, comparisons against prior contaminated-data methods, ablations over the contamination ratio and the temperature parameter beta, and evaluation of the adaptive beta variant EPHAD-Ada to test robustness and the contribution of the post-hoc adjustment mechanism.
